CHAPTER 30 - BIOTECHNOLOGY

Introduction

Human beings have used living organisms to make useful products for thousands of years - baking bread, brewing beer and wine, making curd, cheese and vinegar all depend on the activity of microorganisms. These are examples of TRADITIONAL (or old) biotechnology, which uses whole living cells and natural fermentation without any deliberate change to the genetic material. Since the 1970s, however, scientists have learned to cut, join and transfer pieces of DNA from one organism to another. This gave birth to MODERN biotechnology, built on genetic engineering. Biotechnology may be defined as the use of living organisms, cells or their molecules (such as enzymes and DNA) to make products and provide services useful to human beings. The European Federation of Biotechnology describes it as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts of cells and molecular analogues for products and services. Modern biotechnology is a multidisciplinary field that draws on microbiology, biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics, cell biology and chemical engineering.

30.1 SCOPE OF BIOTECHNOLOGY

The scope of biotechnology is enormous. It touches agriculture (better crops and animals), medicine (new drugs, vaccines, diagnostics and gene therapy), industry (enzymes, antibiotics, biofuels), environment (waste treatment, bioremediation) and food processing. The two core techniques that made modern biotechnology possible are (i) GENETIC ENGINEERING - the deliberate alteration of an organism's DNA, and (ii) large-scale culture of cells in a BIOREACTOR to obtain the desired product. Traditional biotechnology differs from modern biotechnology in one key respect: traditional methods let nature take its course and do not touch the genes, whereas modern methods change the genetic make-up of the organism in a precise, pre-planned way. A GENETICALLY MODIFIED ORGANISM (GMO), also called a transgenic organism, is one whose DNA has been altered by introducing one or more genes from another organism.

30.2 GENETIC ENGINEERING (RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY)

GENETIC ENGINEERING is the technology of changing the genetic material (DNA) of an organism by adding, removing or altering particular genes. Its central technique is RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY, in which a piece of DNA (a gene of interest) from one organism is joined to the DNA of a carrier molecule (a vector) to form a RECOMBINANT DNA molecule, which is then introduced into a host cell where it multiplies and expresses. The recombinant DNA molecule made in this way did not exist before in nature - it is a new combination of genes.

THE TOOLS OF GENETIC ENGINEERING

(a) RESTRICTION ENDONUCLEASES (molecular scissors). These are enzymes obtained from bacteria that cut DNA at specific base sequences called RECOGNITION SITES (usually palindromic sequences of 4 to 8 base pairs). They are named after the bacterium from which they are isolated - for example EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli and BamHI from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens. A restriction enzyme scans the DNA, binds to its recognition sequence and cuts the two strands. Many of them (like EcoRI) cut the two strands at slightly different points, leaving short single-stranded overhangs called STICKY ENDS (or cohesive ends). Because sticky ends are complementary, DNA fragments from two different sources cut by the SAME enzyme have matching sticky ends and can pair with each other - this is what makes recombination possible. Enzymes that cut both strands at the same point leave BLUNT ENDS. Restriction enzymes are called the molecular scissors of genetic engineering.

(b) DNA LIGASE (molecular glue). Once the gene of interest and the vector have been cut with the same restriction enzyme, their complementary sticky ends are brought together and the enzyme DNA LIGASE seals the nicks by forming phosphodiester bonds, joining the two pieces permanently into one recombinant molecule. If restriction enzymes are the scissors, ligase is the glue.

(c) VECTORS (gene carriers / cloning vehicles). A VECTOR is a DNA molecule that can carry the foreign gene into a host cell and replicate independently inside it. A good vector must have (i) an ORIGIN OF REPLICATION (ori) so it can multiply in the host, (ii) a SELECTABLE MARKER (usually an antibiotic-resistance gene) to identify the cells that have taken up the vector, and (iii) one or more unique restriction sites where the foreign DNA can be inserted. The most commonly used vectors are PLASMIDS - small, circular, self-replicating pieces of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome. Other vectors include bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria), cosmids and, for plants, the Ti plasmid of the soil bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which is natures own genetic engineer. The plasmid pBR322 is a classic laboratory cloning vector.

30.3 STEPS OF RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY

Making a recombinant DNA molecule and getting a useful product from it involves the following main steps.
1. ISOLATION OF THE GENETIC MATERIAL (DNA). The cell is broken open (using enzymes such as lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells or protease to remove proteins) and the DNA is separated from proteins, RNA and other molecules. Chilled ethanol is added and the purified DNA precipitates out as fine white threads.
2. CUTTING THE DNA AT SPECIFIC SITES. Both the source DNA (containing the gene of interest) and the vector DNA are cut with the SAME restriction endonuclease so that both carry the same complementary sticky ends.
3. INSERTION OF THE GENE INTO THE VECTOR (ligation). The cut gene of interest and the cut (open) vector are mixed; their sticky ends base-pair and DNA ligase joins them to form the recombinant DNA molecule.
4. INTRODUCTION OF RECOMBINANT DNA INTO THE HOST. The recombinant vector is transferred into a host cell (often the bacterium Escherichia coli). A host cell that takes up foreign DNA is said to be TRANSFORMED. Uptake can be helped by treating cells with calcium ions and a brief heat shock, by ELECTROPORATION (short electric pulses that open pores in the membrane), by a gene gun (biolistics) that fires DNA-coated micro pellets, or by using a microinjection needle.
5. SELECTION AND CLONING OF THE TRANSFORMED HOST (recombinants). Only a few cells actually take up the recombinant DNA. Selectable markers (antibiotic-resistance genes) are used to pick out the transformed cells: when grown on a medium containing the antibiotic, only cells carrying the vector survive. These selected cells are then multiplied (cloned), and because every daughter cell carries a copy of the gene, a large population of identical cells - a CLONE - is obtained, each making the desired product.

30.4 KEY TECHNIQUES

POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION (PCR). PCR is a technique to make millions of copies of a specific segment of DNA in a test tube - a process called AMPLIFICATION. It was devised by Kary Mullis. Each cycle has three steps: (i) DENATURATION - heating to about 94-95 C to separate the double-stranded DNA into single strands; (ii) ANNEALING - cooling to about 50-60 C so that two short chemically synthesised PRIMERS bind to the ends of the target sequence; and (iii) EXTENSION - a heat-stable DNA polymerase called TAQ POLYMERASE (from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus) adds nucleotides and synthesises new strands. Because each new strand becomes a template in the next cycle, the amount of DNA roughly DOUBLES every cycle, so about 30 cycles give more than a billion copies. PCR is used in molecular diagnosis of diseases, DNA fingerprinting, gene cloning and detecting pathogens.

GEL ELECTROPHORESIS (separation of DNA). This technique separates DNA fragments according to their SIZE. The mixture of fragments is loaded into wells at one end of a slab of AGAROSE gel and an electric field is applied. Because DNA is negatively charged (owing to its phosphate groups), the fragments move towards the positive electrode (anode). Smaller fragments move FASTER and therefore travel FARTHER, while larger fragments move slower and stay near the wells. The separated fragments form distinct bands, which are made visible by staining with ETHIDIUM BROMIDE and viewing under ultraviolet light. The separated DNA bands can be cut out of the gel and used for further work - a step called ELUTION. Gel electrophoresis is essential in DNA fingerprinting and in checking the products of restriction digestion and PCR.

THE BIOREACTOR AND DOWNSTREAM PROCESSING. To obtain a product in useful amounts, the recombinant cells must be grown on a large scale. A BIOREACTOR (or fermenter) is a large vessel (often thousands of litres) in which cells or microbes are grown under controlled conditions of temperature, pH, oxygen (aeration), agitation and nutrient supply to obtain the desired product. The most common design is the STIRRED-TANK bioreactor, which has a stirrer to mix and aerate the culture, and probes to monitor conditions. After the reaction is complete, the product must be separated and purified. All the processes carried out AFTER the biosynthesis is over - separation of cells, purification of the product, and its formulation with preservatives to give a market-ready form, together with quality control - are together called DOWNSTREAM PROCESSING.

30.5 APPLICATIONS IN AGRICULTURE

GENETICALLY MODIFIED (TRANSGENIC) CROPS. Plants into which a foreign gene has been introduced are called genetically modified (GM) or transgenic crops. They have been engineered mainly for pest resistance, herbicide tolerance, disease and stress resistance, and improved nutrition.
- Bt COTTON and Bt BRINJAL. The soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) makes a protein (the Bt toxin or Cry protein) that kills certain insects. The gene coding for this toxin (for example cry1Ac) has been introduced into cotton and brinjal so that the plant makes its own insecticide and resists pests such as the bollworm - reducing the need for chemical sprays. In India Bt cotton is grown commercially, while Bt brinjal has been developed but its commercial release is under a moratorium.
- GOLDEN RICE. This is a transgenic rice engineered to make BETA-CAROTENE (a precursor of vitamin A) in its grains, which turns them golden. It was developed to combat vitamin A deficiency, a cause of blindness in many poor countries.
- HERBICIDE-RESISTANT and PEST-RESISTANT crops let farmers control weeds and insects more easily; other GM work aims at drought and salt tolerance and longer shelf life (for example the Flavr Savr tomato).

PLANT TISSUE CULTURE AND MICROPROPAGATION. Tissue culture is the growing of cells, tissues or organs on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled conditions. It rests on TOTIPOTENCY - the capacity of a single plant cell to divide and regenerate a whole plant. A small piece of tissue (the EXPLANT) is placed on a medium containing nutrients and plant hormones (auxins and cytokinins); it forms an undifferentiated mass called CALLUS, which is then induced to form shoots and roots and finally a complete plantlet. Producing thousands of genetically identical plants (clones) in a short time from a small tissue is called MICROPROPAGATION. Growing plants from a single cell or callus free of virus (using the disease-free meristem) gives VIRUS-FREE plants. Tissue culture is used to multiply elite, disease-free planting material of banana, orchids, sugarcane and many ornamentals.

30.6 APPLICATIONS IN MEDICINE AND INDUSTRY

RECOMBINANT INSULIN (HUMULIN). Diabetics need insulin. Earlier insulin was extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs; this animal insulin sometimes caused allergies. Using recombinant DNA technology, the human insulin gene was introduced into the bacterium Escherichia coli, which then produced human insulin. This human insulin made by bacteria is called HUMULIN. It is identical to human insulin, is produced in large amounts and does not cause allergy - the first commercially made recombinant human protein.

RECOMBINANT VACCINES. Traditional vaccines use killed or weakened (attenuated) whole pathogens. Genetic engineering allows the making of safer SUBUNIT vaccines, in which only the gene for a harmless surface protein (antigen) of the pathogen is introduced into yeast or bacteria, which then make large amounts of that antigen. The HEPATITIS B vaccine, made in yeast, is a well-known recombinant vaccine. Such vaccines carry no risk of infection and can be produced cheaply in bulk.

GENE THERAPY. Gene therapy is the correction of a genetic disease by inserting a normal, functioning gene into the cells of a patient who carries a defective one. The first successful clinical gene therapy (1990) was given to a girl suffering from ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) DEFICIENCY, a disorder of the immune system caused by a faulty gene. A functional copy of the gene is introduced (often using a viral vector) so that the cells can make the missing enzyme.

MOLECULAR DIAGNOSIS. Diseases can be detected very early - before symptoms appear - using molecular methods. PCR can detect tiny amounts of a pathogen's DNA or a mutation; the ELISA test detects antigens or antibodies; and DNA PROBES (short labelled single-stranded DNA that binds a complementary sequence) locate specific genes or pathogens. These allow accurate early diagnosis of infections and inherited disorders.

TRANSGENIC ANIMALS. Animals carrying a foreign gene are called transgenic animals. They are used to study how genes work and to make useful proteins. Transgenic cows and sheep have been made to secrete valuable human proteins (such as clotting factors or alpha-1-antitrypsin) in their MILK - an approach nicknamed 'molecular pharming'. The mouse is the most common transgenic animal used in research.

INDUSTRIAL BIOTECHNOLOGY. On an industrial scale, microbes are grown by FERMENTATION to make many products. ANTIBIOTICS such as penicillin (from the mould Penicillium) and streptomycin are made this way. Many ENZYMES used in industry - amylases, proteases and lipases in detergents, rennet substitutes in cheese, pectinases in fruit-juice clarification - are microbial products. Fermentation also makes organic acids (citric acid, acetic acid), alcohol (ethanol as a biofuel), vitamins and single-cell protein.

30.7 BIOFERTILISERS AND BIOPESTICIDES

BIOFERTILISERS are living organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. The chief examples are nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium (in the root nodules of legumes) and free-living Azotobacter and the cyanobacterium (blue-green alga) Anabaena and Azolla in rice fields; and MYCORRHIZA (a symbiosis between fungi and plant roots) that helps the plant absorb phosphorus. They are a cheap, eco-friendly substitute for chemical fertilisers. BIOPESTICIDES are biological agents used to control pests and diseases in place of chemical pesticides. Examples include Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), the fungus Trichoderma and the baculoviruses (NPV), and the neem-based products. Biofertilisers and biopesticides reduce pollution and are central to sustainable, organic farming.

30.8 BIOSAFETY, ETHICAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES

The power to alter genes raises safety and ethical questions. BIOSAFETY means the safe handling of GMOs and the assessment of any risk they may pose to human health and the environment - for example, whether a GM crop might harm non-target insects, transfer its genes to wild relatives, or become a weed. In India, the release of GMOs is regulated by the GENETIC ENGINEERING APPRAISAL COMMITTEE (GEAC), which examines proposals and decides on the safety and use of genetically modified organisms. BIOPIRACY is the unauthorised use and exploitation of the biological resources and the traditional knowledge of a country or community by others (often multinational companies) without proper permission or benefit-sharing - as in the attempts to patent products of neem, turmeric and basmati rice. A PATENT is an exclusive legal right granted to an inventor over an invention; patenting of life forms and genes raises deep ethical concerns. ETHICAL issues also include the safety of eating GM foods, the welfare of transgenic animals, and fairness in who benefits from the new technology. To address these concerns many countries have set up ethics committees and regulatory bodies, and the CARTAGENA PROTOCOL provides an international framework for the safe transfer and use of living modified organisms.

SUMMARY

- Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their molecules to make useful products and services. Traditional biotechnology (bread, curd, wine) does not alter genes; modern biotechnology is built on genetic engineering and large-scale culture in bioreactors.
- Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technology) joins a gene of interest to a vector to make recombinant DNA. Its tools are restriction endonucleases (molecular scissors, giving sticky ends), DNA ligase (molecular glue) and vectors (mainly plasmids, also phages and the Ti plasmid).
- The steps are: isolate DNA, cut it with a restriction enzyme, insert the gene into a vector by ligation, introduce the recombinant DNA into a host (transformation), then select and clone the recombinant cells using selectable markers.
- PCR amplifies DNA a billion-fold using denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by Taq polymerase. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size (small fragments move farther towards the anode). A bioreactor grows cells on a large scale; downstream processing separates, purifies and formulates the product.
- In agriculture: Bt cotton and Bt brinjal (pest resistance), golden rice (vitamin A), and herbicide-tolerant crops; tissue culture and micropropagation (based on totipotency) give many identical, virus-free plants.
- In medicine: recombinant insulin (humulin) from E. coli, recombinant (subunit) vaccines such as hepatitis B, gene therapy (first used for ADA deficiency), molecular diagnosis (PCR, ELISA, DNA probes) and transgenic animals. In industry: antibiotics, enzymes and other products by fermentation.
- Biofertilisers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria, mycorrhiza) and biopesticides (Bt, Trichoderma, baculoviruses) support sustainable farming.
- Biosafety, biopiracy, patents and other ethical and social issues are overseen in India by the GEAC and internationally by frameworks such as the Cartagena Protocol.

chapter_summary.title: Biotechnology - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary covers biotechnology - its meaning and scope, the tools and steps of genetic engineering, key techniques (PCR, gel electrophoresis and bioreactors), and its applications in agriculture, medicine and industry, along with biosafety and ethical issues.

sections.heading: Scope of biotechnology
bullets: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their molecules to make useful products and services.
Traditional biotechnology (bread, curd, cheese, wine) uses natural fermentation and does NOT alter the genes.
Modern biotechnology is built on genetic engineering and large-scale culture in bioreactors.
A genetically modified organism (GMO) or transgenic organism has DNA altered by introducing genes from another organism.

sections.heading: Tools and steps of genetic engineering
bullets: Restriction endonucleases are the molecular scissors; they cut DNA at specific recognition sites, often leaving sticky (cohesive) ends.
DNA ligase is the molecular glue that seals the gene of interest into the vector to make recombinant DNA.
Vectors (mainly plasmids, also phages and the Ti plasmid) carry the gene into the host and must have an origin of replication and a selectable marker.
Steps: isolate DNA, cut with a restriction enzyme, insert the gene into the vector, introduce it into a host (transformation), then select and clone the recombinants.

sections.heading: Key techniques
bullets: PCR amplifies a target DNA a billion-fold using cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by heat-stable Taq polymerase.
Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size; being negatively charged they move to the anode and smaller fragments travel farther.
A bioreactor grows cells on a large scale under controlled temperature, pH, oxygen and stirring.
Downstream processing covers all separation, purification, formulation and quality control done after biosynthesis.

sections.heading: Applications in agriculture
bullets: Bt cotton and Bt brinjal carry a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis and make their own insecticidal toxin, resisting pests.
Golden rice is engineered to make beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A) to combat vitamin A deficiency.
Herbicide-tolerant and disease-resistant transgenic crops are also being developed.
Tissue culture (based on totipotency) and micropropagation give many identical, virus-free plants from a small explant.

sections.heading: Applications in medicine and industry; biosafety
bullets: Recombinant insulin (humulin) is made by E. coli carrying the human insulin gene; recombinant vaccines (e.g. hepatitis B) are safe subunit vaccines.
Gene therapy corrects a genetic defect (first used for ADA deficiency); molecular diagnosis uses PCR, ELISA and DNA probes.
Industrial fermentation makes antibiotics, enzymes and organic acids; biofertilisers and biopesticides support sustainable farming.
Biosafety, biopiracy and patents are ethical/social issues; in India the GEAC regulates the release of GMOs.

key_takeaways: Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or their molecules to make useful products; traditional methods do not alter genes, modern methods do.
Genetic engineering joins a gene of interest to a vector using restriction enzymes (scissors, sticky ends) and DNA ligase (glue) to form recombinant DNA.
The steps are: isolate DNA, cut, insert into a vector, introduce into a host (transformation), and select and clone recombinant cells with selectable markers.
PCR amplifies DNA (denature, anneal, extend with Taq polymerase); gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size; bioreactors and downstream processing scale up and purify products.
In agriculture: Bt cotton/brinjal, golden rice and herbicide-tolerant crops, plus tissue culture and micropropagation based on totipotency.
In medicine and industry: recombinant insulin, vaccines, gene therapy, molecular diagnosis, transgenic animals, fermentation products, biofertilisers and biopesticides.

glossary.definition: The use of living organisms, cells or their molecules (such as enzymes and DNA) to make products and provide services useful to human beings.
The technology of deliberately changing the genetic material (DNA) of an organism by adding, removing or altering particular genes.
A new DNA molecule formed by joining a gene of interest from one organism to the DNA of a vector; it did not exist before in nature.
A bacterial enzyme (molecular scissors) that cuts DNA at a specific recognition sequence, often leaving sticky ends; e.g. EcoRI.
Short single-stranded overhangs left when a restriction enzyme cuts the two DNA strands at different points; complementary ends allow fragments to join.
The enzyme (molecular glue) that joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, sealing the gene into the vector.
A DNA molecule such as a plasmid that carries a foreign gene into a host cell and replicates there; needs an origin of replication and a selectable marker.
A small, circular, self-replicating piece of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the chromosome, widely used as a cloning vector.
The uptake of foreign (recombinant) DNA by a host cell, which then carries and expresses the introduced gene.
A technique that amplifies a specific DNA segment a billion-fold using cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by Taq polymerase.
A technique that separates DNA fragments by size in an agarose gel under an electric field; negatively charged DNA moves to the anode.
A large vessel in which cells or microbes are grown under controlled conditions to obtain a product on a large scale.
A genetically modified organism (plant or animal) that carries a foreign gene introduced by recombinant DNA technology.
Human insulin produced by the bacterium Escherichia coli carrying the human insulin gene; the first commercial recombinant human protein.
The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, the Indian body that assesses biosafety and regulates the release of genetically modified organisms.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Biotechnology (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer short-answer questions in 2-4 sentences and long-answer questions with clearly labelled steps or points. Draw simple labelled sketches where helpful.

questions.question: Define biotechnology and distinguish between traditional and modern biotechnology with one example of each.
questions.answer: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their molecules (such as enzymes and DNA) to make products and services useful to human beings. Traditional biotechnology uses whole cells and natural fermentation WITHOUT altering the genes - for example making curd, bread or wine. Modern biotechnology is based on genetic engineering (changing the DNA) and large-scale culture in bioreactors - for example making human insulin (humulin) in bacteria.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the key contrast: genes untouched vs genes altered, with examples.

questions.question: Why are restriction endonucleases called 'molecular scissors'? What are sticky ends?
questions.answer: Restriction endonucleases are enzymes that recognise a specific base sequence (recognition site) in DNA and cut both strands there - so they act like scissors that cut DNA at chosen points. Many of them (e.g. EcoRI) cut the two strands at slightly different positions, leaving short single-stranded overhangs called STICKY (cohesive) ends. Because these overhangs are complementary, DNA fragments cut by the same enzyme can pair and be joined together.
questions.explanation: Cutting at specific sites = scissors; unequal cut leaves complementary single-strand overhangs = sticky ends.

questions.question: Describe the main steps involved in making a recombinant DNA molecule and obtaining a product from it.
questions.answer: The main steps are: (1) ISOLATION OF DNA - the cell is broken open and DNA is separated from proteins and RNA and precipitated with chilled ethanol. (2) CUTTING - both the source DNA (carrying the gene of interest) and the vector are cut with the SAME restriction enzyme, giving matching sticky ends. (3) INSERTION (ligation) - the gene and the cut vector are mixed; their sticky ends pair and DNA ligase joins them into a recombinant DNA molecule. (4) INTRODUCTION INTO A HOST - the recombinant vector is put into a host such as E. coli (transformation), aided by calcium ions and heat shock, electroporation or a gene gun. (5) SELECTION AND CLONING - selectable markers (antibiotic-resistance genes) identify the transformed cells, which are then multiplied to give a clone that makes the desired product, recovered by downstream processing.
questions.explanation: The five standard steps: isolate, cut, ligate, transform, select and clone.

questions.question: Name the three steps of one cycle of PCR and state the role of Taq polymerase.
questions.answer: One PCR cycle has three steps: (1) DENATURATION - heating to about 94-95 C separates the double-stranded DNA into single strands; (2) ANNEALING - cooling to about 50-60 C lets two short primers bind to the ends of the target sequence; (3) EXTENSION - the enzyme adds nucleotides to make new strands. Taq polymerase is the heat-stable DNA polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus) that carries out the extension step; being heat-stable it survives the high denaturation temperature.
questions.explanation: Denaturation, annealing, extension; Taq is the heat-stable polymerase that copies DNA.

questions.question: In gel electrophoresis, why do smaller DNA fragments move farther, and towards which electrode does DNA move?
questions.answer: DNA carries a negative charge because of its phosphate groups, so in the electric field it moves towards the POSITIVE electrode (anode). The agarose gel acts like a sieve: smaller fragments pass through the pores of the gel more easily and therefore move FASTER and travel FARTHER, while larger fragments are held back and stay nearer the wells. Thus fragments separate into bands according to their size.
questions.explanation: Negative DNA moves to the anode; gel sieves so small fragments go farther.

questions.question: What is Bt cotton? How does it resist insect pests?
questions.answer: Bt cotton is a transgenic (genetically modified) cotton that carries a gene (e.g. cry1Ac) taken from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. This gene codes for a protein called the Bt toxin (Cry protein). The plant therefore makes its own insecticidal protein, which kills insect pests such as the bollworm when they feed on it. As a result the crop resists pests and needs far fewer chemical insecticide sprays.
questions.explanation: Bt gene from Bacillus thuringiensis makes the plant produce insect-killing Cry toxin.

questions.question: What is micropropagation? On which property of plant cells is it based?
questions.answer: Micropropagation is the production of thousands of genetically identical plants (clones) in a short time by growing small pieces of tissue on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled conditions. It is based on TOTIPOTENCY - the ability of a single plant cell to divide and regenerate into a whole plant. A small explant forms a callus, which is induced to form shoots and roots and finally complete plantlets.
questions.explanation: Mass clonal propagation from tissue culture; rests on totipotency.

questions.question: How is human insulin (humulin) produced by biotechnology, and why is it better than insulin from animals?
questions.answer: The human insulin gene is introduced into the bacterium Escherichia coli using recombinant DNA technology; the bacterium then makes human insulin, which is grown on a large scale in a bioreactor and purified. This bacterial human insulin is called HUMULIN. It is better than the older insulin extracted from cattle and pig pancreas because it is identical to human insulin, can be made in large amounts, and does not cause the allergic reactions that animal insulin sometimes did.
questions.explanation: Human gene in E. coli makes identical, plentiful, allergy-free insulin.

questions.question: Evaluate the biosafety and ethical issues raised by biotechnology. Mention the role of GEAC and the meaning of biopiracy.
questions.answer: Biotechnology is powerful but raises biosafety and ethical concerns. BIOSAFETY is about the safe handling of GMOs and assessing their risks to health and the environment - for example, a GM crop might harm non-target insects, pass its genes to wild relatives, or become a weed; there are also worries about the safety of eating GM foods. ETHICAL concerns include the welfare of transgenic animals and fairness in who benefits from the technology. BIOPIRACY is the unauthorised use of a country's biological resources and traditional knowledge by others without permission or benefit-sharing (as in attempts to patent neem, turmeric and basmati). PATENTING of genes and life forms is itself ethically debated. In India the GENETIC ENGINEERING APPRAISAL COMMITTEE (GEAC) assesses biosafety and decides on the release of GMOs, and the international Cartagena Protocol governs the safe transfer of living modified organisms. On balance, biotechnology offers great benefits but must be used under careful regulation.
questions.explanation: Weigh risks/benefits; define biosafety, biopiracy, patents; role of GEAC and Cartagena Protocol.

questions.question: Define biotechnology.
questions.answer: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their molecules (such as enzymes and DNA) to make products and provide services that are useful to human beings. It is a multidisciplinary field drawing on microbiology, biochemistry, genetics and engineering.
questions.explanation: State the definition and note it is multidisciplinary.

questions.question: Give two differences between traditional and modern biotechnology.
questions.answer: 1. Traditional biotechnology uses whole cells and natural fermentation without changing the genes (e.g. curd, wine), whereas modern biotechnology deliberately alters the DNA by genetic engineering. 2. Traditional methods are usually small-scale and age-old, while modern biotechnology grows engineered cells on a large scale in bioreactors to make products such as humulin.
questions.explanation: Contrast gene alteration and scale/technique.

questions.question: What is a vector? State two features a good cloning vector must have.
questions.answer: A vector is a DNA molecule (such as a plasmid) that carries a foreign gene into a host cell and can replicate there. A good vector must have (i) an origin of replication so it can multiply in the host, and (ii) a selectable marker (usually an antibiotic-resistance gene) so that cells which have taken up the vector can be identified. It should also have unique restriction sites for inserting the gene.
questions.explanation: Definition plus origin of replication and selectable marker.

questions.question: Name the two kinds of ends produced when restriction enzymes cut DNA.
questions.answer: Restriction enzymes may produce STICKY (cohesive) ends - short single-stranded overhangs that are complementary and can join with other fragments cut by the same enzyme - or BLUNT ends, produced when the enzyme cuts both strands at the same point leaving no overhang.
questions.explanation: Sticky (cohesive) ends and blunt ends.

questions.question: Why must the gene of interest and the vector be cut with the same restriction enzyme?
questions.answer: Using the same restriction enzyme ensures that both the gene of interest and the vector are cut at identical sequences, producing the SAME kind of complementary sticky ends. These matching sticky ends can then base-pair with each other, allowing DNA ligase to join the gene into the vector. If different enzymes were used the ends would not be complementary and would not join.
questions.explanation: Same enzyme gives complementary sticky ends that can pair.

questions.question: List, in order, the five main steps of recombinant DNA technology.
questions.answer: (1) Isolation of the DNA from the cell. (2) Cutting the source DNA and the vector with the same restriction enzyme. (3) Insertion of the gene of interest into the vector by ligation to form recombinant DNA. (4) Introduction of the recombinant DNA into a host cell (transformation). (5) Selection and cloning of the transformed (recombinant) cells using selectable markers.
questions.explanation: Isolate, cut, ligate/insert, transform, select and clone.

questions.question: Name three methods by which foreign DNA can be introduced into a host cell.
questions.answer: Foreign DNA can be introduced by: (1) treating cells with calcium ions followed by a brief heat shock; (2) ELECTROPORATION, where short electric pulses make the membrane temporarily porous; and (3) the GENE GUN (biolistics), which fires DNA-coated micro-pellets into the cells. Microinjection is another method used for animal cells.
questions.explanation: Calcium/heat-shock, electroporation, gene gun (or microinjection).

questions.question: How are transformed cells selected from non-transformed cells after introducing recombinant DNA?
questions.answer: The vector carries a selectable marker, usually an antibiotic-resistance gene. After the DNA is introduced, the cells are grown on a medium containing that antibiotic. Only the cells that have taken up the vector (and its resistance gene) can survive and grow; the non-transformed cells, lacking resistance, are killed. The surviving colonies are therefore the transformed cells, which are then multiplied (cloned).
questions.explanation: Antibiotic-resistance marker + antibiotic medium selects transformed cells.

questions.question: What is PCR and why is it important?
questions.answer: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is a technique that makes millions of copies of a specific DNA segment in a test tube - a process called amplification. Each cycle involves denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by Taq polymerase, and the DNA roughly doubles each cycle. PCR is important because it lets scientists obtain enough DNA from a tiny sample for gene cloning, DNA fingerprinting and the molecular diagnosis of diseases.
questions.explanation: Amplification technique; uses in cloning, fingerprinting, diagnosis.

questions.question: Explain the principle of gel electrophoresis.
questions.answer: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. The fragments are loaded into wells in an agarose gel and an electric field is applied. Because DNA is negatively charged (due to phosphate groups) it moves towards the positive electrode (anode). The gel acts as a molecular sieve, so smaller fragments move faster and travel farther, while larger fragments lag behind. The separated fragments appear as bands, made visible with ethidium bromide under UV light.
questions.explanation: Charge drives DNA to anode; gel sieves by size; small go farther.

questions.question: What is downstream processing?
questions.answer: Downstream processing includes all the steps carried out AFTER the biosynthesis (the reaction in the bioreactor) is complete. It covers separating the cells, purifying the desired product, and formulating it (with suitable preservatives) into a market-ready form, together with quality control tests. It is essential for turning the culture output into a usable product.
questions.explanation: Post-synthesis separation, purification, formulation, quality control.

questions.question: Why is Taq polymerase, rather than an ordinary DNA polymerase, used in PCR?
questions.answer: PCR repeatedly heats the reaction to about 94-95 C during the denaturation step of every cycle. An ordinary DNA polymerase would be destroyed (denatured) by such high temperatures and would have to be added afresh each cycle. Taq polymerase, isolated from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is HEAT-STABLE and remains active through repeated heating, so the whole reaction can be automated without adding fresh enzyme.
questions.explanation: Repeated high temperature needs a heat-stable enzyme.

questions.question: What are transgenic crops? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Transgenic (genetically modified) crops are plants into which a foreign gene has been introduced by recombinant DNA technology to give a useful new trait such as pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or better nutrition. Two examples are Bt cotton (which carries a Bacillus thuringiensis gene for pest resistance) and golden rice (engineered to make beta-carotene, a source of vitamin A).
questions.explanation: Definition plus Bt cotton and golden rice.

questions.question: Explain how a Bt crop protects itself against insect pests.
questions.answer: A Bt crop carries a gene (e.g. cry1Ac) taken from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. This gene codes for the Bt toxin (Cry protein). The plant therefore makes this insecticidal protein in its own tissues. When an insect pest such as the bollworm feeds on the plant, the toxin acts on its gut and kills it. Thus the crop is protected without needing heavy chemical spraying.
questions.explanation: Plant expresses Bt/Cry toxin that kills feeding pests.

questions.question: What is tissue culture? Name one advantage of micropropagation.
questions.answer: Tissue culture is the growing of plant cells, tissues or organs on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled conditions, relying on the totipotency of plant cells. An explant forms a callus, which then regenerates shoots, roots and whole plantlets. One advantage of micropropagation is that thousands of genetically identical, disease-free plants can be produced quickly from a small amount of tissue.
questions.explanation: Definition; advantage = many identical, disease-free plants fast.

questions.question: How is recombinant insulin produced, and why is it preferred over animal insulin?
questions.answer: The human insulin gene is inserted into the bacterium Escherichia coli using recombinant DNA technology; the bacteria then make human insulin, which is grown in bioreactors and purified (this product is humulin). It is preferred over insulin extracted from cattle and pig pancreas because it is identical to human insulin, can be produced in large amounts, and does not cause the allergic reactions that animal insulin sometimes did.
questions.explanation: Human gene in E. coli; identical, plentiful, allergy-free.

questions.question: What is gene therapy? Give the first disease it was used to treat.
questions.answer: Gene therapy is the treatment of a genetic disease by inserting a normal, functioning copy of a gene into the cells of a patient who has a defective one, so that the cells can make the missing product. The first successful gene therapy, carried out in 1990, was for a girl suffering from ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) DEFICIENCY, an immune disorder caused by a faulty gene.
questions.explanation: Insert a normal gene to correct a defect; first used for ADA deficiency.

questions.question: What are biofertilisers? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Biofertilisers are living organisms that enrich the nutrient content of the soil in an eco-friendly way, chiefly by fixing atmospheric nitrogen or by helping absorb phosphorus. Two examples are Rhizobium, a nitrogen-fixing bacterium living in the root nodules of legumes, and the cyanobacterium Anabaena (with Azolla) used in rice fields. Mycorrhiza (fungus-root association) is another example that improves phosphorus uptake.
questions.explanation: Living soil-enrichers; e.g. Rhizobium and Anabaena/Azolla.

questions.question: What are biopesticides? Give one example.
questions.answer: Biopesticides are biological agents (living organisms or their products) used to control pests and diseases in place of chemical pesticides, making farming more eco-friendly. One example is Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), whose toxin kills insect pests; others include the fungus Trichoderma and the baculoviruses (NPV).
questions.explanation: Biological pest-control agents; e.g. Bt (or Trichoderma).

questions.question: What is biopiracy? Give one example.
questions.answer: Biopiracy is the unauthorised use and exploitation of the biological resources and traditional knowledge of a country or community by others (often multinational companies) without proper permission or fair benefit-sharing. Examples include the attempts to patent products or uses of neem, turmeric and basmati rice, which are part of Indian traditional knowledge.
questions.explanation: Unauthorised use of bioresources/knowledge; e.g. neem, turmeric, basmati.

questions.question: Why is biosafety important in biotechnology, and what is the role of GEAC?
questions.answer: Biosafety is important because genetically modified organisms could pose risks - a GM crop might harm non-target insects, transfer its genes to wild relatives, become a weed, or raise concerns about the safety of GM food. Biosafety means assessing and managing such risks so that GMOs are handled and released safely. In India the GENETIC ENGINEERING APPRAISAL COMMITTEE (GEAC) examines proposals and decides on the safety, approval and release of genetically modified organisms.
questions.explanation: Manage ecological/health risks; GEAC assesses and approves GMO release.

questions.question: Starting from a single DNA molecule, roughly how many copies are produced after 10 PCR cycles, and why?
questions.answer: In each PCR cycle the target DNA is copied so that the amount roughly DOUBLES. Starting from one molecule, after n cycles there are about 2^n copies. After 10 cycles this is 2^10 = 1024, i.e. about a thousand copies. This exponential doubling is why about 30 cycles can produce more than a billion copies from a very small starting sample.
questions.explanation: Doubling each cycle gives 2^n; 2^10 is about 1024.

questions.question: Describe the three main types of tools used in genetic engineering and the role of each.
questions.answer: Genetic engineering uses three main kinds of molecular tools. (1) RESTRICTION ENDONUCLEASES (molecular scissors): bacterial enzymes that recognise a specific base sequence (recognition site) and cut DNA there, often leaving complementary sticky ends; they are named after the bacterium of origin (e.g. EcoRI from E. coli). They let us cut out the gene of interest and open the vector at chosen points. (2) DNA LIGASE (molecular glue): the enzyme that joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, sealing the gene of interest into the vector to make a recombinant DNA molecule. (3) VECTORS (gene carriers): DNA molecules such as plasmids (also bacteriophages and the Ti plasmid) that carry the foreign gene into the host and replicate there; a good vector has an origin of replication, a selectable marker and unique restriction sites. Together, scissors cut, glue joins, and vectors carry the gene into the cell.
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, vectors carry; give features and examples.

questions.question: Explain the steps of recombinant DNA technology, taking the production of human insulin as an example.
questions.answer: (1) ISOLATION: the human insulin gene (the gene of interest) and a plasmid vector are obtained, and DNA is isolated and purified. (2) CUTTING: both the insulin gene and the plasmid are cut with the SAME restriction enzyme, giving matching sticky ends. (3) INSERTION: the insulin gene and the cut plasmid are mixed; their sticky ends pair and DNA ligase joins them into a recombinant plasmid carrying the insulin gene. (4) INTRODUCTION INTO HOST: the recombinant plasmid is introduced into Escherichia coli (transformation), for example using calcium ions and heat shock. (5) SELECTION AND CLONING: transformed bacteria are selected using an antibiotic-resistance marker and then multiplied on a large scale in a bioreactor. The bacteria express the gene and make human insulin, which is then recovered and purified by downstream processing to give humulin. This shows how the general steps produce a useful medical product.
questions.explanation: Apply isolate-cut-insert-transform-select to insulin, ending in humulin.

questions.question: Explain the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), describing the three steps of a cycle and two uses of PCR.
questions.answer: PCR is a technique for amplifying (making millions of copies of) a specific DNA segment in vitro. Each cycle has three steps. (1) DENATURATION: the reaction is heated to about 94-95 C so the double-stranded DNA separates into two single strands. (2) ANNEALING: it is cooled to about 50-60 C so that two short synthetic primers bind (anneal) to the ends of the target sequence on the single strands. (3) EXTENSION: the heat-stable Taq polymerase adds nucleotides to the primers and synthesises new complementary strands. Because each new strand acts as a template in the next cycle, the amount of DNA roughly doubles every cycle, so about 30 cycles give over a billion copies. Two uses of PCR are: the molecular diagnosis of diseases (detecting a pathogen or a mutation from a tiny sample) and DNA fingerprinting for identification and forensic work.
questions.explanation: Denaturation, annealing, extension; exponential doubling; two uses.

questions.question: Describe how genetically modified crops and plant tissue culture are used in agriculture, with examples.
questions.answer: Biotechnology helps agriculture in two main ways. GENETICALLY MODIFIED (transgenic) CROPS carry a foreign gene giving a useful trait. Bt cotton and Bt brinjal carry a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis so the plant makes its own insecticidal Cry toxin and resists pests such as the bollworm, cutting the need for chemical sprays. Golden rice is engineered to make beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A) to fight vitamin A deficiency, and other crops are made herbicide-tolerant or disease- and stress-resistant. PLANT TISSUE CULTURE grows cells or tissues on a sterile nutrient medium; based on totipotency, a small explant forms a callus that regenerates whole plantlets. MICROPROPAGATION uses this to produce thousands of identical, disease-free plants quickly (e.g. banana, orchids, sugarcane), and virus-free plants can be raised from meristem tips. Together these techniques raise yield, quality and disease resistance.
questions.explanation: Transgenic crops (Bt, golden rice) plus tissue culture/micropropagation with examples.

questions.question: Describe four applications of biotechnology in medicine.
questions.answer: (1) RECOMBINANT INSULIN: the human insulin gene is expressed in E. coli to make humulin, an allergy-free human insulin available in large amounts for diabetics. (2) RECOMBINANT VACCINES: only the gene for a harmless surface antigen of a pathogen is expressed in yeast or bacteria to make a safe subunit vaccine, such as the hepatitis B vaccine, which carries no risk of infection. (3) GENE THERAPY: a normal gene is introduced into a patient with a genetic defect so the cells can make the missing product; it was first used successfully for ADA deficiency. (4) MOLECULAR DIAGNOSIS: diseases are detected very early using PCR (to detect a pathogens DNA or a mutation), ELISA and DNA probes. Transgenic animals that secrete useful human proteins in their milk are a further medical application.
questions.explanation: Insulin, vaccines, gene therapy, molecular diagnosis (plus transgenic animals).

questions.question: Discuss the biosafety, ethical and social issues associated with biotechnology and how they are addressed.
questions.answer: Biotechnology brings great benefits but also concerns. BIOSAFETY issues concern the possible harm of GMOs: a GM crop might damage non-target insects, transfer its genes to wild relatives, become a weed, or raise doubts about the safety of eating GM food. ETHICAL issues include the welfare of transgenic animals, the acceptability of altering life, and fairness in who gains from the technology. SOCIAL and legal issues include BIOPIRACY - the unauthorised use of a nations bioresources and traditional knowledge (as in attempts to patent neem, turmeric and basmati) - and the PATENTING of genes and life forms, which many consider unethical. These concerns are addressed by regulation and ethics oversight: in India the GENETIC ENGINEERING APPRAISAL COMMITTEE (GEAC) assesses biosafety and approves the release of GMOs, laws protect traditional knowledge, and the international CARTAGENA PROTOCOL governs the safe transfer of living modified organisms. Thus the technology can be used responsibly if properly regulated.
questions.explanation: Cover biosafety, ethics, biopiracy/patents; GEAC, laws, Cartagena Protocol.

questions.question: Describe the applications of biotechnology in industry, including the role of the bioreactor.
questions.answer: In industry, useful microbes are grown by FERMENTATION on a large scale in BIOREACTORS - vessels that provide controlled temperature, pH, oxygen (aeration), stirring and nutrients so cells can grow and make the desired product efficiently. This is used to make ANTIBIOTICS such as penicillin (from the mould Penicillium) and streptomycin, and many ENZYMES - amylases, proteases and lipases used in detergents, rennet substitutes for cheese, and pectinases for clarifying fruit juice. Fermentation also produces organic acids (citric acid, acetic acid), alcohol (ethanol used as a biofuel), vitamins and single-cell protein. After biosynthesis, DOWNSTREAM PROCESSING separates, purifies and formulates the product with quality control. Recombinant DNA technology has further improved industrial strains so they give higher yields.
questions.explanation: Fermentation in bioreactors for antibiotics, enzymes, acids, biofuel; downstream processing.

questions.question: A forensic scientist has only a trace of DNA from a crime scene. Explain how PCR and gel electrophoresis together help in identification.
questions.answer: The trace of DNA is far too little to analyse directly, so PCR is used first to AMPLIFY it. Chosen primers target specific regions; through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension by Taq polymerase, the amount of DNA doubles each cycle, giving millions of copies of the target regions from the tiny sample. The amplified DNA is then cut (or already sized regions) and loaded onto an AGAROSE GEL for electrophoresis. Under the electric field the negatively charged fragments move towards the anode, with smaller fragments travelling farther, so the fragments separate into a pattern of bands according to size. The band pattern (DNA fingerprint) from the crime-scene sample is compared with patterns from suspects; a match at the band positions indicates the fragments are of the same sizes and the samples may share the same source. Thus PCR provides enough DNA and electrophoresis reveals the identifying pattern.
questions.explanation: PCR amplifies the trace; electrophoresis separates by size to give a comparable band pattern.

questions.question: A village woman makes curd by adding a spoon of old curd to warm milk, while a nearby factory makes human insulin by inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria. (a) Which process is traditional biotechnology and which is modern? (b) In which process are genes deliberately altered? (c) Name the bacterium used to make insulin.
questions.answer: (a) Making curd is traditional biotechnology; making insulin in bacteria is modern biotechnology. (b) Genes are deliberately altered only in the modern process (inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria); curd making does not change any gene. (c) The bacterium used to make insulin is Escherichia coli.
questions.explanation: Distinguish traditional vs modern; gene alteration; host = E. coli.

questions.question: In a lab, a gene of interest and a plasmid are both treated with the enzyme EcoRI, and then mixed with another enzyme that seals them together. (a) What type of enzyme is EcoRI? (b) Why are both cut with the same enzyme? (c) Name the sealing enzyme.
questions.answer: (a) EcoRI is a restriction endonuclease (molecular scissors) obtained from Escherichia coli. (b) Both the gene and the plasmid are cut with the same enzyme so that they get the same complementary sticky ends, which can base-pair and join together. (c) The sealing enzyme is DNA ligase, which joins the fragments to form recombinant DNA.
questions.explanation: Restriction enzyme; same enzyme gives matching sticky ends; ligase seals.

questions.question: A student lists steps to make a recombinant microbe: cut DNA, isolate DNA, select recombinants, insert gene into vector, put vector into host. (a) Write the steps in the correct order. (b) What is the entry of DNA into the host called? (c) How are recombinant cells selected?
questions.answer: (a) Correct order: isolate DNA -> cut DNA -> insert gene into vector (ligation) -> put vector into host -> select recombinants. (b) The entry (uptake) of the recombinant DNA into the host cell is called transformation. (c) Recombinant (transformed) cells are selected using a selectable marker, usually an antibiotic-resistance gene: only transformed cells survive on a medium containing that antibiotic.
questions.explanation: Order the steps; transformation; antibiotic-resistance selection.

questions.question: A technician runs a PCR machine that repeatedly heats to 95 C, cools to 55 C, and warms to 72 C. (a) Name the three steps at these temperatures. (b) Which enzyme works at 72 C? (c) Why must this enzyme be heat-stable?
questions.answer: (a) 95 C = denaturation (strands separate); 55 C = annealing (primers bind); 72 C = extension (new strands are synthesised). (b) Taq polymerase (DNA polymerase) works at the 72 C extension step. (c) It must be heat-stable because the reaction is heated to about 95 C in every cycle; an ordinary enzyme would be destroyed, but heat-stable Taq survives repeated heating so the process can be automated.
questions.explanation: Match temperatures to steps; Taq at extension; heat stability needed.

questions.question: In a gel-electrophoresis experiment, DNA samples are loaded in wells at the negative end and current is switched on; after some time distinct bands appear along the gel. (a) Towards which electrode does DNA move and why? (b) Which fragments travel farthest? (c) How are the bands made visible?
questions.answer: (a) DNA moves towards the positive electrode (anode) because DNA is negatively charged owing to its phosphate groups. (b) The smallest fragments travel farthest because they pass through the pores of the gel most easily. (c) The bands are made visible by staining the gel with ethidium bromide and viewing it under ultraviolet (UV) light, under which the stained DNA fluoresces.
questions.explanation: Anode because DNA is negative; small fragments farthest; ethidium bromide/UV.

questions.question: A cotton farmer suffers heavy losses from bollworm and sprays costly insecticides. He is advised to grow Bt cotton. (a) From which organism is the Bt gene taken? (b) How does Bt cotton protect itself? (c) State one benefit to the farmer.
questions.answer: (a) The Bt gene is taken from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. (b) Bt cotton carries this gene and so makes its own insecticidal protein (the Bt/Cry toxin); when the bollworm feeds on the plant the toxin kills it. (c) A benefit to the farmer is that far less chemical insecticide is needed, which lowers cost and reduces environmental pollution while protecting the yield.
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis; plant makes Cry toxin; less spraying/cost.

questions.question: A nursery wants thousands of identical, disease-free banana plants quickly from one healthy plant. They use a small piece of tissue grown on a nutrient medium. (a) Name this technique. (b) On which property of cells is it based? (c) What is the mass production of such plants called?
questions.answer: (a) The technique is plant tissue culture. (b) It is based on totipotency - the ability of a single plant cell to divide and regenerate into a complete plant. (c) The rapid mass production of many genetically identical plants in this way is called micropropagation.
questions.explanation: Tissue culture; totipotency; micropropagation.

questions.question: A child with diabetes earlier used insulin from pig pancreas and sometimes developed allergy. The doctor now prescribes humulin. (a) What is humulin? (b) In which organism is it made? (c) Why does it not cause allergy?
questions.answer: (a) Humulin is human insulin produced by recombinant DNA technology. (b) It is made in the bacterium Escherichia coli, into which the human insulin gene has been introduced. (c) It does not cause allergy because it is identical to the insulin naturally made in the human body, unlike the slightly different animal (pig or cattle) insulin that could trigger allergic reactions.
questions.explanation: Humulin = recombinant human insulin; made in E. coli; identical to human insulin.

questions.question: A farmer replaces chemical fertiliser with Rhizobium inoculant for his legume crop and uses Bacillus thuringiensis instead of chemical pesticide. (a) What is Rhizobium acting as here? (b) How does it help the crop? (c) What is Bacillus thuringiensis acting as?
questions.answer: (a) Rhizobium is acting as a biofertiliser. (b) It lives in the root nodules of the legume and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use, thus enriching the soil and supplying nitrogen naturally. (c) Bacillus thuringiensis is acting as a biopesticide, controlling insect pests biologically in place of chemical pesticide.
questions.explanation: Rhizobium = biofertiliser (nitrogen fixation); Bt = biopesticide.

questions.question: A foreign company files a patent to use turmeric for healing wounds - a use long known in Indian households - and a new GM crop is proposed for release in India. (a) What is the wrongful patenting of such traditional knowledge called? (b) Which Indian body must clear the GM crop for release? (c) State one biosafety concern about releasing a GM crop.
questions.answer: (a) The wrongful use and patenting of a countrys bioresources and traditional knowledge (like the turmeric example) is called biopiracy. (b) The GM crop must be cleared for release by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC). (c) One biosafety concern is that the GM crop might harm non-target insects or transfer its genes to wild relatives (or become a weed), so its ecological safety must be assessed before release.
questions.explanation: Biopiracy; GEAC clears release; a genuine ecological biosafety risk.
